# Cloudflare OS: An AI productivity environment

Cloudflare OS is an "operating system" for AI productivity originally developed for use inside Cloudflare. A large portion of Cloudflare's workforce -- from engineering to sales and everything in between -- uses Cloudflare OS every day to help them do their jobs.

![A Q3 planning workspace in Cloudflare OS, with an AI-generated slide deck](docs/images/q3-planning-workspace.png)

This is not a traditional computer operating system. We use the term "operating system" in two senses:

* An operating system for *the company* to be productive with AI, in a way that is safe, so that the security team can sleep at night.
* An operating system for AI workloads, analogous to the sense in which a traditional operating system manages compute workloads.

Cloudflare OS provides three things in particular:

1. An agent chat UI where you can ask agents to do tasks, preloaded with knowledge about how your company operates.
2. Sandboxed application development, so that you can ask agents to build "gadgets" (small personal apps) and safely share what you've built with others.
3. A security framework, called Gatekeepers, that applies guardrails to both agents and apps such that non-technical users can safely "go nuts" and nothing bad will happen.

We are making Cloudflare OS open source so that others can copy it and customize it for their own company. The idea is not that your company uses Cloudflare OS, but rather that you make it "*Your Company* OS".

## Quick Start

To quickly run Cloudflare OS locally, [install pnpm](https://pnpm.io/), then do:

    pnpm run-local

Then visit: http://localhost:8787

This runs the whole stack locally on wrangler and workerd. This is not meant for production use, but is a quick way to see what the product does.

Alternatively, you can [deploy to your Cloudflare account](https://os.cloudflare.app/deploy).

(More options at the end of this readme.)

### What to try

Try prompts like:

* "Make slides for my upcoming meeting with a customer." (This will use the built-in slides blueprint.)
* "Make a collaborative whiteboard app." (This will create a new app from scratch.)
* "Make a tic tac toe game." followed by "I'll be X and you be O. I've made my first move. Your turn."
* "Make an issue dashboard for this GitHub repo." (Attach a repo; requires that the GitHub integration is configured.)
* "Fix the typos in this Google Doc." (Attach a doc; requires that the Google integration is configured.)

### WARNING: Early access

Cloudflare OS is in a state of heavy development. This repository is actually version 2, a complete rewrite taking what we learned from version 1 and putting it on a new foundation.

As of the August 2026 release, Cloudflare OS v2 is very capable, but still has many rough edges. We know, and we're working on it. For now, consider this an "early access" release.

## Overview: What is Cloudflare OS really?

### Gadgets: A new way of thinking about software

Cloudflare OS is more than just another chatbox with connectors. The system revolves around a new approach to software, where every user runs their own copy of the productivity apps they use.

When you create a slide deck in Cloudflare OS, you are not calling out to some SaaS software running in the cloud. The system creates a *private instance* of the slide deck software *just for you*. We call this a "gadget". This instance runs in a separate sandbox from everyone else's slide decks.

This has two profound effects:
1. It's impossible for the slide deck app to have a security bug that leaks your slides to an attacker. The Cloudflare OS sandbox controls all access to your private instance of the app.
2. If you want, you can freely modify the code. If the slide deck app is missing a feature you need, you can just ask your agent to add it. And because of point 1, it's totally safe to do so.

This is a big departure from the last 25 years of cloud architecture and "Software as a Service", but we think AI has changed the equation. When any user is capable of prompting an agent to add the features they need, the centralized model of software stops making sense.

### Gatekeepers: A capability-based security layer

Gatekeepers are like supercharged MCP servers.

When you introduce an agent or Gadget to an external resource, a Gatekeeper is created to manage that access. The Gatekeeper is a piece of software specific to each external service which moderates a Gadget's connection to that service. It:
* Provides a clean Cap'n Web API to the service (wrapping whatever API the service provides natively).
* Handles authorization (e.g. via OAuth).
* Enforces narrow access to only the specific resource the user intended.
* Logs every action the Gadget (or agent) performs, for your review.
* For any action which has side effects, provides the human user an opportunity to approve or deny the action ("human in the loop").

On the last point, Gatekeepers implement a significant advancement in the state of the art. Traditionally, human-in-the-loop setups require the human to approve actions *synchronously*. When the agent wants to do something, it has to *stop* and wait for said approval before it can continue. This is annoying: you give your agent a task, then walk away and get a coffee, only to come back and find the agent got stuck on an approval on the first step and has made no progress. As a result, people often give in and set their agents to "auto-approve", or `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which is, obviously, unsafe.

Gatekeepers provide a better way: When the agent (or Gadget) performs an action that requires approval, the Gatekeeper will *simulate* the outcome locally, allowing the agent to proceed and queue up more actions. The Gatekeeper tells the agent that the action completed, and if the agent tries to read back the results, the Gatekeeper gives it simulated results. Once the agent is done, the user may approve or reject the actions in bulk, or one-by-one, but either way, they can do it later, when it is convenient.

Logistically, each Gatekeeper is implemented as a separate Worker. In the future, we envision Gatekeeper services being deployed and maintained independently from OS instances, but the details have yet to be worked out. For now, we have provided a few interesting Gatekeepers in this repository which you can deploy together with your own OS instance.

### Think of an office suite

The basic user experience of Cloudflare OS is something like an online office suite, like Google Docs or MS Office. But, imagine that instead of a fixed set of file types (document, spreadsheet, slide deck), each file -- or "Gadget" -- is potentially its own custom application, written by AI to serve exactly your needs.

Just like office docs, each gadget is private by default, but can be shared -- securely -- in order to collaborate with your team or your friends.

Just like office docs, you can have thousands of them. You can create them on a whim.

Just like office docs, you can start from "templates" -- called "Blueprints". But where an office template is just some content, a Blueprint specifies a whole application.

Like office docs, you can create new templates (blueprints) from your own docs (Gadgets) and share them with others. But when you do so, you are sharing the code for a whole app.

### It kind of is an Operating System

The OS terminology isn't *entirely* marketing. Cloudflare OS is actually analogous to an operating system on a technical level.

| Normal OS      | Cloudflare OS              |
|----------------|----------------------------|
| kernel         | packages/workshop-backend  |
| device drivers | packages/gatekeeper-*      |
| shell          | packages/workshop-frontend |
| processes      | gadgets                    |
| executables    | blueprints                 |
| users          | users                      |
| ACLs           | shared permissions         |
| ???            | agents                     |

Our "kernel" is in the workshop-backend package. The backend legitimately does a lot of things similar to real OS kernels: it connects users to programs and devices (Gadgets and Gatekeepers, as we call them) while implementing security by sandboxing applications and enforcing access control.

In this analogy, Gatekeepers -- which connect users and agents to external services -- are like drivers -- which connect users and programs to external devices.

There is one thing that traditional OSes don't really manage today, but Cloudflare OS does: AI agents. If you think about it, this is really a missing feature in traditional OSes. We believe that AI agents cannot simply be treated as users. They must be accountable to a human user, while at the same time having their own restricted permissions. Agents do work by writing snippets of code and executing them on the fly. The ideal security model for all of this is capability-based security, not access control lists. See what I mean? Perhaps traditional OSes ought to give AI agents special treatment, too.

### Built on Workers, by the Workers team

Cloudflare OS is built on [Cloudflare Workers](https://workers.cloudflare.com), making heavy use of [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/), [Dynamic Workers](https://blog.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/), and [Facets](https://blog.cloudflare.com/durable-object-facets-dynamic-workers/) in particular. Every workspace is its own Durable Object, every Gadget runs in a Dynamic Worker Facet, and Gatekeepers also install facets into each workspace to manage access to remote services.

Cloudflare OS is, in fact, built by the very people who built Workers itself. It uses cutting-edge features of the Workers Runtime -- in fact, Dynamic Workers, Facets, and several other features were added to the runtime specifically to support Cloudflare OS, with more to come. Studying the Cloudflare OS source code is a great way to understand how the Workers Runtime team thinks Workers should be used.

Being built on Workers does not mean that Cloudflare OS can only run on Cloudflare. In fact, [`workerd`, the Cloudflare Workers Runtime, is itself open source](https://github.com/cloudflare/workerd), and Cloudflare OS can run entirely on top of it on your own servers.

## Features

### General multi-purpose agent

The Cloudflare OS coding agent is actually a fully multi-purpose agent that can perform arbitrary tasks; like other popular coding agents, you don't have to code with it. You can use it to build Gadgets, but you can also skip the Gadget and just have the agent perform tasks directly. The Cloudflare OS agent is a [Code Mode](https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode/) agent -- it performs tasks by writing and immediately executing snippets of code. It can be connected to external resources using Gatekeepers (like MCP -- see below).

### Build apps with AI

While you can code a Gadget by hand if you want, the expectation is that AI writes the code for you. Cloudflare OS features a built-in coding agent that will build whatever you ask it, test it for you, and debug errors.

You can choose your LLM. Cloudflare OS works with many major AI model providers and self-hosted models, with more providers being added all the time.

Because of the tightly-integrated and simplified nature of the platform, even when using the same underlying AI models, the Cloudflare OS coding agent often performs better and faster with fewer tokens than a general-purpose coding agent would.

### Collaborate with AI

Every app built with Cloudflare OS automatically has an agent-friendly API. That means, after you've asked AI to build the app, you can also ask AI to collaborate with you *inside* the app. No need to build an MCP server nor integrate a custom agent loop. It's just there by default.

This works because the client and server portions of a Gadget are required to communicate via [Cap'n Web RPC](https://github.com/cloudflare/capnweb). This is a win-win:
1. Cap'n Web is extremely low-boilerplate, which makes it easy for agents to work with. You basically just define a method on your server, then call it from your client, as if it were a local call.
2. Meanwhile, it means that the server necessarily exposes an easy-to-understand API which could be called directly by an agent. The AI Agent harness uses [Code Mode](https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode/) for tool calling, making it trivial to expose the Gadget's API directly for the agent to invoke.

### Real-time Multiplayer

You can share your Gadget just like you'd share a document in a typical online office suite. You can give specific users access, or create a share link that provides access to anyone who opens it. And just like those online office suites, you'll be able to see your collaborators' actions in real time.

This works because every Gadget is backed by a [Durable Object](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/), Cloudflare's stateful serverless primitive which makes real-time multiplayer collaboration easy. It's so easy that the coding agent just implements it by default, without being asked.

### Blueprints: Share your code

If you've created a Gadget that might be useful to others, but you don't want to share the Gadget itself, you can instead share a Blueprint, allowing other people to create their own copy of the Gadget. A Blueprint is essentially a copy of the code.

It may sound simple, but Blueprints are a major change from cloud software tradition. Traditionally, if you create a web app that you want to share with other users, you host the app on your server, and the users connect to that. Blueprints are much more like mobile apps and traditional PC apps: every user runs their own copy of the software.

In the age of AI, this change is critically important. On one hand, AI empowers an individual developer to build more than ever, but it is still difficult for an individual developer to maintain an online service; this eliminates the need. On the other hand -- and even more importantly -- allowing each user to run their own copy of the software empowers the user to *change* the software to meet their needs, using AI. No need to file a feature request, no need to beg the developer to prioritize it. The end user can solve their own problems.

### Sandboxed and secure by default

Each Gadget runs in a secure sandbox that prevents it from talking to the internet at all without your explicit consent. In particular:
* The server runs in a [Dynamic Worker](https://blog.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/) which has had its access to the internet disabled. It can only communicate with specific external resources that you have explicitly designated, via [Workers Bindings](https://blog.cloudflare.com/workers-environment-live-object-bindings/).
* The client code runs in a sandboxed iframe. This iframe can communicate with its server only via a Cap'n Web RPC session provided over `postMessage()` to the parent frame. The iframe is otherwise blocked from accessing the internet (to the maximum extent allowed by browsers, via `Content-Security-Policy` and iframe sandbox settings).

### Capability-based access control

Each agent, and each Gadget, by default has access to nothing. Even if you've configured the Gadget Workshop with access to external accounts, agents and Gadgets do NOT automatically get to use them.

Instead, you must *introduce* each agent (or Gadget) to any particular resources you want it to access. For instance, you may introduce a GitHub repository by pasting a link to it, or clicking "add resource" and selecting it via the UI. An agent can also request an introduction to a resource it thinks it needs, which you can then provide or deny.

This differs from most agent harnesses, where MCP servers are configured upfront, making broad access to all your services ambiently available to the agent in every chat. Capability-based introductions keep each agent restricted to only the access it actually needs for the job at hand.

## Get Started

### Deploy to your Cloudflare account

We've built an online flow that helps you deploy to your own Cloudflare account:

https://os.cloudflare.app/deploy

Or, for more sophisticated deployment, with your gatekeepers and potentially code changes, check out our deployment starter repo:

https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-os-starter

### Run locally

To quickly run Cloudflare OS locally, [install pnpm](https://pnpm.io/), then do:

    pnpm run-local

Then visit: http://localhost:8787

This runs Cloudflare OS using `wrangler`, the Workers developer tooling CLI. This is not the right way to run the OS on a production server, but it works fine for trying it out on your local machine.

Your data will be stored in a subdirectory named `.wrangler`.

### Deploy to your own server using `workerd`

**COMING SOON**

Cloudflare OS can run entirely on `workerd`, Cloudflare's open source runtime for Workers. In fact, the "run locally" instructions above use `workerd` under the hood. We are still working on documentation and tooling to help you smoothly deploy the OS on top of `workerd` on your own servers. If you are feeling adventurous, [read the low-level documentation for workerd config](https://github.com/cloudflare/workerd/blob/main/src/workerd/server/workerd.capnp) (or point your agent at it) and have a go.

#### Configuring external services

Many Gatekeepers require configuration in order to be able to connect to third-party services, including obtaining OAuth client credentials for each service. Unfortunately, many service providers intentionally do not make this easy, since the intended audience for OAuth is developers.

Each gatekeeper package contains instructions for how to set it up:

* [GitHub API](packages/gatekeeper-github/README.md)
* [Google API](packages/gatekeeper-google/README.md)
* [Cloudflare API](packages/gatekeeper-cloudflare/README.md)
* [Supabase API](packages/gatekeeper-supabase/README.md)
* [Notion API](packages/gatekeeper-notion/README.md)
* [Confluence API](packages/gatekeeper-confluence/README.md)
* [Email Workers](packages/gatekeeper-email/README.md)
* [Home Assistant](packages/gatekeeper-homeassistant/README.md)
* [Slack API](packages/gatekeeper-slack/README.md)
* [Spotify](packages/gatekeeper-spotify/README.md)
* [ZoomInfo API](packages/gatekeeper-zoominfo/README.md)

## Developing

When developing, you'll want to run the front-end and back-end as two separate commands in two terminals:

    pnpm dev-server
    pnpm dev-client

Then visit: http://localhost:3000

### Contributing

At this time, we are not seeking outside contribution.

AI has made writing code easy. The hard part, today, is not writing the code, but reviewing it, making sure quality stays high, and keeping the product coherent. In that light, unfortunately, external code contributions are "donating" the easy part of the job, while creating more of the hard work.

With that said, we are happy to accept small, trivially-verified PRs that fix a problem. However, we ask that you refrain from submitting low-value PRs (e.g. typo fixes) or PRs that are more than a dozen or so lines. Such PRs will be closed with a reference to this guideline.

If you have a big idea you'd like us to consider, feel free to [open a discussion](https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-os/discussions) about it.

This policy may change in the future as the project matures. Until then, thank you for your understanding.

## Credits

Cloudflare OS has far too many open source dependencies to list here. But, we'd like to highlight a few that do particularly heavy lifting:

* [Pi](https://pi.dev/) (specifically, `pi-agent-core`), which made it easy to support every LLM provider with one API.
* [CodeMirror](https://codemirror.net/) provides our code editor UI and operational transform implementation for synchronizing real-time edits.
* [isomorphic-git](https://isomorphic-git.org/) is used to implement the backing storage for Gadget code and integration with external git servers.
* [Vite](https://vite.dev/), which makes the development loop so pleasant.

1: // This file defines the API spoken between the Gadgets Workshop service and the front-end UI.
2: //
3: // The UI is a good old "fat client" SPA. Why not use SSR? Because:
4: // - Users of this UI are likely to have it open often, maybe even all the time. Startup time is
5: //   less of a concern than with sites you visit only briefly, and assets are likely to be in cache
6: //   in any case.
7: // - The Gadgets themselves are sandboxed on the client side in addition to the server side. This
8: //   sandboxing requires running code in the browser. It is not plausible to server-side render
9: //   a Gadget itself.
10: // - By providing a really clean API boundary between client and server, we make it easier to build
11: //   alternative clients.
12: // - SPA is just easier to think about.
13: //
14: // The entire API between the client and server is an RPC API, using Cloudflare's JavaScript RPC,
15: // which essentially allows natural JavaScript / TypeScript interfaces to be exposed over the
16: // network.
17: //
18: // The RPC interface operates over a WebSocket, which the client starts immediately at startup and
19: // keeps open for the entire lifetime of the session, reconnecting if needed.
20: //
21: // Gadgets run inside a sandboxed iframe which has no ability to talk to the outside world at all,
22: // except postMessage() to the parent frame. Through postMessage() exchanges, the Gadget can speak
23: // RPC to the Workshop. Among other things, through this interface, the Workshop provides the
24: // Gadget a stub pointing to the Gadget's server-side Durable Object interface.

1: // This file defines the API that the AI Gadgets Workshop uses to talk to Adapters. Each Adapter
2: // provides connectivity to some external service which AI Gadgets can then manipulate. Each
3: // installation of the Gadgets Workshop may have access to different adapters, typically based on
4: // the set of internal services used at the particular company.
5: //
6: // For instance, there might be adapters for Google Workspace, GitHub, Jira, etc.
7: //
8: // Adapters provide access to resources. For instance, a Google Workspace adapter might provide
9: // access to Google Docs, Spreadsheets, Gmail mailboxes, etc. Each Google Doc, for example, is a
10: // separate "resource". Adapters are designed to provide object-oriented, capability-based access
11: // to such resources, enabling the Gadget Workshop to grant a particular Gadget fine-grained
12: // access to just the things the user wants that Gadget to access.
13: //
14: // Each adapter is deployed as a completely independent Workers application from the Gadgets
15: // Workshop itself, and is provided to the Workshop as a service binding. The Workshop communicates
16: // with the adapter over JavaScript RPC. The types in this file define that RPC interface. The
17: // `Adapter` type is the root interface implemented by the service binding.

121:  * on every turn where compaction never reaches it. A gatekeeper is expected to return far fewer than

272:  * asking to connect "https://github.com/owner/repo/" would match no resource and the accept modal
273:  * would open with nothing pre-selected.

428: /**
429:  * The root interface of an Adapter, as provided to the Gadget Workshop.
430:  *
431:  * An installation of the Gadget Workshop is provided with a set of Adapters to allow it to
432:  * interface with other services.
433:  * Options for GatekeeperVendor.connectAccount(). `scopes` selects the access tier (see that
434:  * method). `resourceUrlPatterns`, if given, limits the connection to the authorization needed for
435:  * those grantable resource types; if omitted, authorization for all the vendor's resource types
436:  * is requested. An **empty array is meaningful and distinct from omitting it**: it requests no
437:  * resource authorization at all, which is how a caller connects an account for a non-resource
438:  * purpose (e.g. billing) without asking the user to grant data access it will never use.
439:  */
440: export type GatekeeperConnectOptions = {
441:   scopes?: "auth" | "full";
442:   resourceUrlPatterns?: string[];
443: };
444: 
445: export interface GatekeeperVendor extends WorkerEntrypoint {
446:   /** Get display info for the service, suitable for display to a user. */
447:   describe(): Promise<VendorDescription>;
448: 
449:   /**
450:    * Start the auth flow to connect to the user's remote account. Returns the URL which the user
451:    * should open in their browser in order to complete the flow. This URL will be opened in a new
452:    * tab; when it completes, it should close itself using window.close().
453:    *
454:    * When the flow completes, `callback.complete()` should be called to add the connection to the
455:    * user's list of authorizations. (`callback` can be stored.)
456:    *
457:    * A typical implementation creates a UserAccount Durable Object to manage the authorization
458:    * flow, storing the callback in its storage, then directing the user to a URL that references
459:    * the DO. Once the user completes the flow, the DO invokes the callback. The DO should set an
460:    * alarm to delete itself after some timeout if the user fails to complete the flow.
461:    *
462:    * SECURITY: The returned URL must include a cryptographic nonce (in addition to the DO ID) to
463:    * prevent replay attacks. The nonce should be stored in the DO and verified when the user visits
464:    * the URL. See gatekeeper-google for a reference implementation.
465:    *
466:    * `options.scopes` selects how much access to request (default "full"):
467:    *   - "full": the gatekeeper's full capability scopes (repos, docs, etc.). The resulting
468:    *     connection is persisted as a usable connected account.
469:    *   - "auth": only the minimal scopes needed to verify the user's email for sign-in. The grant is
470:    *     transient — after `complete()` lets the caller read getAuthenticatedEmail(), the gatekeeper
471:    *     discards it. Vendors without `providesAuth` ignore this and always use their full scopes.
472:    *
473:    * `options.resourceUrlPatterns`, if given, limits the connection to the authorization needed for
474:    * those grantable resource types. If omitted, authorization for all of the vendor's resource
475:    * types is requested. An empty array is not the same as omitting it: it requests no resource
476:    * authorization, so a vendor must treat `[]` as "none" rather than falling back to "all" -- doing
477:    * otherwise would silently over-request access the user was never shown a reason for.
478:    */
479:   connectAccount(callback: Fetcher<GatekeeperConnectCallback>,
480:                  options?: GatekeeperConnectOptions): Promise<{url: string}>;
481: 
482:   /**
483:    * Get the list of resource types this vendor supports. Each entry describes a category of
484:    * resource the vendor can provide access to, along with a URL pattern for matching.
485:    *
486:    * `options.userId` specifies the user ID (usually, email address) of the user who is driving the
487:    * query, which the gatekeeper can consider in deciding what resources are available. If it
488:    * returns an empty list, then the gatekeeper will be totally hidden from the user.
489:    *
490:    * TODO: Providing the user ID here is a temporary hack to enable a hidden internal gatekeeper.
491:    *   Later on we should come up with a better way to manage which users see which gatekeepers.
492:    *
493:    * TODO: How does the Gadget Workshop know when the supported URLs have changed, without polling?
494:    */
495:   getSupportedResources(options?: {userId?: string}): Promise<SupportedResource[]>;
496: 
497:   /**
498:    * Returns TypeScript source code defining all types covering APIs defined by this Gatekeeper.
499:    * The returned string is the content of a `.d.ts` file. All types refereced by
500:    * `ResourceDescription` must be exported by this file. The types should ideally have complete
501:    * JSDoc comments describing them.
502:    *
503:    * The Gadgets system will parse this file to construct a type database, which will be made
504:    * available to the coding agent in a way that supports progressive discovery.
505:    *
506:    * TODO: Define exactly what global types and imports are available. I suppose capnweb should be
507:    * importable, but is anything else needed?
508:    * TODO: How does the Gadget Workshop know when the types have changed, without polling?
509:    * TODO: Should we somehow distinguish stable vs. unstable types? Unstable are safe to use in
510:    *   one-off situations only.
511:    */
512:   getTypeScriptTypes(): Promise<string>;
513: 
514:   /**
515:    * Mint a NEW connected account, with no OAuth flow. Safe to expose on this public interface: it
516:    * only *creates* accounts — it cannot look up or return an existing account — and it takes no
517:    * arguments, so it carries no user identity. The Workshop persists the returned account (like an
518:    * OAuth-connected account) and treats it as the authority thereafter. Present only on vendors that
519:    * set VendorDescription.autoProvisionsAccount; callers gate on that flag rather than probing, since
520:    * RPC stubs cannot report optional-method presence.
521:    */
522:   createAccount?(): Promise<Fetcher<GatekeeperUser>>;
523: }

525: export interface GatekeeperConnectCallback extends WorkerEntrypoint {
526:   /**
527:    * Indicates the connection completed successfully.
528:    *
529:    * `expiresAt`, if provided, indicates when the credentials are expected to stop being
530:    * refreshable. Do not pass the expiry of a short-lived access token if the gatekeeper can
531:    * refresh it transparently; that token-cache expiry is internal to the gatekeeper. This allows
532:    * the Workshop to proactively show the account as expired in the UI without waiting for an
533:    * operation to fail. If not provided, the system relies on the gatekeeper calling
534:    * `credentialsExpired()` when a refresh or authorization failure is detected.
535:    */
536:   complete(user: Fetcher<GatekeeperUser>, expiresAt?: Date): Promise<void>;
537: 
538:   // Note: If the authorization flow fails, the error can be displayed directly to the user, and
539:   // the callback can be discarded.
540: 
541:   /**
542:    * Called when the gatekeeper discovers that credentials have expired or been revoked (e.g., a
543:    * token refresh fails with an authorization error). The Workshop records this and notifies
544:    * subscribers so the UI can reflect the expired state.
545:    *
546:    * The gatekeeper should avoid calling this repeatedly -- once is sufficient. Subsequent calls
547:    * are harmless but redundant.
548:    */
549:   credentialsExpired(): Promise<void>;
550: 
551:   /**
552:    * Called when credentials have been restored (e.g., after a reconnect flow completes).
553:    * `expiresAt` is the new expected refreshability expiration date, if known.
554:    */
555:   credentialsRestored(expiresAt?: Date): Promise<void>;
556: }

558: /**
559:  * RPC interface to an Adapter. This is a privileged interface exposed to the Gadget Workshop UI
560:  * itself, not to Gadgets nor AI agents.
561:  *
562:  * The Adapter is already specialized for a particular human user of the Gadget Workshop. The
563:  * Adapter capability itself represents permission to access all of the user's data that is
564:  * available through it, so needs to be guarded carefully. Hence, only the Workshop itself should
565:  * ever have direct access to an Adapter object.
566:  */
567: export interface GatekeeperUser extends WorkerEntrypoint {
568:   /** Get display info for an account, suitable for display to a user. */
569:   describe(): Promise<AccountDescription>;
570: 
571:   /**
572:    * Typically returns the same as GatekeeperVendor.getSupportedResources(), though an
573:    * implementation could choose to return a narrower set if the specific account does not support
574:    * every resource that the vendor supports generally.
575:    */
576:   getSupportedResources(): Promise<SupportedResource[]>;
577: 
578:   /**
579:    * Get a Durable Object class that can implement a gatekeeper for the given resource. This class
580:    * can be used to instantiate a Facet which implements the Gatekeeper interface.
581:    *
582:    * Note that the Overseer of a Gadget will call this immediately when the user pastes in a URL,
583:    * *before* the user has actually chosen to grant the Gadget any permissions on the resource.
584:    * Permissions are requested by instantiating the Gatekeeper and calling setPermissions() on it,
585:    * usually after first calling describe() to find out what the resource can do.
586:    *
587:    * The returned class is imbued (via `ctx.props`) with the user's credentials and the resource
588:    * ID. The returned `resource` indicates which SupportedResource matched the URL.
589:    */
590:   getGatekeeperClassFor(url: string): Promise<{
591:     class: DurableObjectClass<Gatekeeper<any>>;
592:     resource: SupportedResource;
593:   }>;
594: 
595:   /**
596:    * Get the UI used to choose a specific resource.
597:    * `resourceUrlPattern` is the `urlPattern` associated with the supported resource.
598:    */
599:   startResourceConfigurator(
600:     resourceUrlPattern: string,
601:   ): Promise<ResourceConfiguratorFrame>;
602: 
603:   /**
604:    * Revoke this account connection. The GatekeeperUser, and all Gatekeepers created through it,
605:    * become broken.
606:    */
607:   revoke(): Promise<void>;
608: 
609:   /**
610:    * Start the flow to refresh/replace credentials on this account. Returns the URL for the user
611:    * to visit in a new tab to complete re-authentication. When the flow completes, the
612:    * GatekeeperConnectCallback (provided during the original connectAccount() flow) will be
613:    * notified via credentialsRestored(). The existing account Fetcher and all gatekeeper bindings
614:    * created through it continue to work with the new credentials.
615:    *
616:    * SECURITY: As with connectAccount(), the returned URL must include a cryptographic nonce to
617:    * prevent replay attacks.
618:    */
619:   reconnect(): Promise<{url: string}>;
620: 
621:   /**
622:    * For vendors that advertise `providesAuth`, returns the account's email address for use as the
623:    * user's sign-in identity. The email MUST be verified by the provider (e.g. Google
624:    * `email_verified`, a GitHub primary+verified email, or a Cloudflare account email) — the
625:    * Workshop keys accounts by email, so an unverified address would allow account takeover.
626:    * Returns null when the account has no verified email or the vendor does not support auth.
627:    */
628:   getAuthenticatedEmail(): Promise<string | null>;
629: 
630:   /** Get a `GatekeeperUserVerifier` representing this user. */
631:   getVerifier(): Promise<Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier>>;
632: 
633:   /**
634:    * Ensure the authorization for the listed grantable resource types (by `urlPattern`) is granted
635:    * on this account, expanding the grant if needed.
636:    *
637:    * Returns the URL for the user to visit to authorize them, or no URL if nothing was needed.
638:    * Gatekeepers with no grantable resource types should return no URL.
639:    *
640:    * SECURITY: As with connectAccount(), any returned URL must include a cryptographic nonce.
641:    */
642:   ensureResources(resourceUrlPatterns: string[]): Promise<{url?: string}>;
643: 
644:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
645:   // Singleton / management-UI capabilities. Present only on accounts created by
646:   // GatekeeperVendor.createAccount() whose describe() sets AccountDescription.singleton and/or
647:   // .providesUi. The Workshop gates calls on those declaration flags rather than probing the stub,
648:   // since RPC stubs cannot reliably report whether an optional method exists.
649: 
650:   /**
651:    * Get a Durable Object class implementing the account's agent singleton, for accounts whose
652:    * describe() sets AccountDescription.singleton. The Workshop installs this gatekeeper into the
653:    * owner's gadgets like any other gatekeeper — as a Facet under the Overseer — and auto-provides
654:    * its session to the agent as an unnamed capsule. Because it is a normal Gatekeeper, the session
655:    * (Gatekeeper.startSession) and catalog (Gatekeeper.getAgentCatalog) run gadget-side in the
656:    * gatekeeper's own worker with no round-trip back through this account DO; every read is still
657:    * authorized as an observation via the ApprovalQueue, exactly like any gatekeeper.
658:    *
659:    * The returned class is imbued (via `ctx.props`) with whatever the account needs to serve the
660:    * singleton (e.g. the account id and sharing domain).
661:    */
662:   getSingletonGatekeeperClass?(): Promise<DurableObjectClass<Gatekeeper<any>>>;
663: 
664:   /**
665:    * The account's full-page management UI (iframe HTML + ui capability). `context.isAdmin` is passed
666:    * fresh per open (not baked into the account) so admin-gated features reflect current status.
667:    */
668:   startAppUi?(context: AppUiContext): Promise<GatekeeperUiFrame>;
669: 
670:   // TODO:
671:   // - Query whether account has scope to access a particular URL.
672: }
673: 
674: /**
675:  * Opaque object representing the capability to verify whether a particular user is able to access
676:  * a particular Gatekeeper. Minted by `GatekeeperUser`, and then passed to
677:  * `Gatekeeper.addObserver()` and possibly other future interfaces.
678:  *
679:  * At present, this interface has no methods, because it is merely meant to be passed back to the
680:  * Gatekeeper that created it.
681:  *
682:  * IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: As of this writing, there is no runtime-supported way to "unwrap" a
683:  * `Fetcher` passed back to its implementer in order to extract the underlying `props`. This will
684:  * be added eventually. For now, we recommend that the `GatekeeperUserVerifier` implement a public
685:  * but non-standard method which the same gatekeeper's `addObserver()` implementations can call.
686:  * The overseer promises only to pass a `GatekeeperUserVerifier` object back to the same gatekeeper
687:  * that created it, so addObserver() can then call that non-standard method and trust the results.
688:  */
689: export interface GatekeeperUserVerifier extends WorkerEntrypoint {}
690: 
691: /**
692:  * Interface exposed by a Gatekeeper instance implementing a specific resource binding on a
693:  * specific Gadget.
694:  *
695:  * The Gatekeeper executes as a Durable Object Facet, where it is a child of the Overseer. This
696:  * interface is exposed to the Overseer, not directly to the Gadget.
697:  */
698: export interface Gatekeeper<Session> extends DurableObject {
699:   /**
700:    * Get more info on the specific resource without actually granting access. This information is
701:    * to be presented to the user in the UI, before the user actually confirms they want to grant
702:    * access.
703:    */
704:   describe(): Promise<ResourceDescription>;
705: 
706:   /**
707:    * Returns the a subset of the type definitions returned by
708:    * GatekeeperVendor.getTypeScriptTypes(), specifically covering types used by this Gatekeeper.
709:    * This allows the agent to be provided with only types relevant to them rather than the entire
710:    * API space of the vendor, which may support many kinds of resources.
711:    */
712:   getTypeScriptTypes(): Promise<string>;
713: 
714:   /**
715:    * Catalog of action kinds this gatekeeper MAY auto-apply without per-action review, for
716:    * pre-approval UIs that must list them before any action has been submitted. Each entry is the
717:    * {tag, label} an action of that kind carries on its ActionDescription.actionKind. This is the
718:    * *potential* set; the per-action `autoApprovable` verdict is still the binding gate at apply
719:    * time. Gatekeepers with no auto-approvable actions return [].
720:    */
721:   getAutoApprovableActions(): Promise<ActionKind[]>;
722: 
723:   /**
724:    * Get the capability representing this resource's RPC interface which will be provided to the
725:    * Gadget.
726:    *
727:    * Every operation performed through this session must be submitted to the approval queue.
728:    * Observations (read-only operations) must be authorized before data is returned to the caller.
729:    * Side-effecting actions must not actually be performed until they are approved.
730:    *
731:    * It is suggested that the gatekeeper "simulate" actions that have not been approved yet, that
732:    * is, the `Session` interface should reflect the state of the resource as if all actions had
733:    * been applied. This allows the Gadget to keep working, potentially queuing up additional
734:    * dependent actions. That said, there is no strict requirement that a gatekeeper does such
735:    * simulation -- it is really up to the gatekeeper author to decide what is appropriate for the
736:    * particular API.
737:    */
738:   startSession(approvalQueue: RpcStub<ApprovalQueue>): Promise<Session>;
739: 
740:   /**
741:    * Bounded, user-specific metadata the agent uses to discover entries reachable through this
742:    * gatekeeper's session, without paging the full session API. Implemented only by gatekeepers
743:    * whose session benefits from a discovery index (e.g. an agent singleton like the Context
744:    * Library); most gatekeepers omit it. Catalog access is an observation, so the implementation
745:    * must authorize it via `authorizer.authorizeObservation()` before returning metadata. Returns
746:    * null when there is no catalog. Return the entries the agent most needs first and pass them
747:    * through `boundAgentCatalog()`, since both that clamp and the Workshop's drop from the tail.
748:    */
749:   getAgentCatalog?(
750:     authorizer: RpcStub<ObservationAuthorizer>,
751:   ): Promise<AgentCatalog | null>;
752: 
753:   /**
754:    * Informs the gatekeeper that a new user is being added to the Gadget with the potential to see
755:    * all data that was read from this Gatekeeper in the past.
756:    *
757:    * `id` is a unique, stable, but opaque string chosen by the overseer to identify this user in
758:    * the context of this gadget.
759:    *
760:    * The gatekeeper must verify that the given user is allowed to directly observe everything that
761:    * has been observed through this gatekeeper in the past. If this is not the case, addObserver()
762:    * must throw an exception.
763:    *
764:    * If this returns without throwing, the Gatekeeper must remember that this user is now an
765:    * observer. If any future observation must be hidden from this observer, then the
766:    * `ObservationDescription` must include the `excludeObservers` property to indicate who is not
767:    * permitted to see the observation.
768:    *
769:    * `addObserver()` may be called again with the same user ID. If so, the gatekeeper should re-run
770:    * the same verifications it would have done if the user were newly-added. The overseer may run
771:    * this periodically to check if the user's access to the resource may have been revoked.
772:    *
773:    * For most gatekeepers, addObserver() should simply check that the user is allowed to read the
774:    * target resource in general -- there's no actual need to check against a log of past
775:    * observations. For gatekeepers that provide broad access to a user's resources, though, it may
776:    * be unlikely that any other user could possibly have access to everything the gatekeeper provides.
777:    * In these cases, logging what was actually observed makes things more useful.
778:    *
779:    * For example, imagine a gatekeeper that grants access to a user's email inbox. Full access to
780:    * an inbox is extremely personal and usually no other user can possibly be permitted such broad
781:    * access. However, if the Gadget itself carefully reads only emails addressed to a particular
782:    * mailing list, then it is OK to reveal those observations to any member of the mailing list.
783:    * The gatekeeper should ideally permit observers who are mailing list members.
784:    */
785:   addObserver(id: string, user: Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier>): Promise<void>;
786: 
787:   /**
788:    * Notifies the gatekeeper that it can stop tracking the given observer, who was previously
789:    * added using `addObserver()`. The gatekeeper no longer needs to verify whether each observation
790:    * is safe for this observer.
791:    *
792:    * This method must be idempotent: If the gatekeeper is unaware that this user was ever added, it
793:    * should just ignore the call rather than throw.
794:    */
795:   removeObserver(id: string): Promise<void>;
796: 
797:   /** Returns the provider for describe().hasSlashCommands, if supported. */
798:   getSlashCommandProvider?(): Promise<SlashCommandProvider>;
799: 
800:   // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
801:   // Callbacks invoked by the overseer to apply (or reject) actions that were previously queued
802:   // for approval via the ApprovalQueue.
803:   //
804:   // Each action is identified by a sequential integer action ID, assigned by the gatekeeper when
805:   // it submits the action for approval. The action ID is passed back to these methods so the
806:   // gatekeeper can look up the action details in its own storage.
807: 
808:   /**
809:    * Action was approved. This call should apply the action (or schedule it to be applied).
810:    *
811:    * If this throws an exception, the user will be informed that the action failed and given the
812:    * opportunity to retry or discard.
813:    *
814:    * Depending on policy conditions, an action may be approved and applied automatically. However,
815:    * the gatekeeper is nevertheless expected to submit all actions for approval; there is no mode
816:    * in which it's OK to skip the check.
817:    */
818:   applyAction(action: number): Promise<void>;
819: 
820:   /**
821:    * Indicates that an action was rejected by the user. The gatekeeper should clean up any
822:    * associated storage.
823:    *
824:    * If the returned `restart` flag is true, rejecting this action requires restarting the Gadget.
825:    * This is sometimes needed by gatekeepers that simulate actions as if they had been approved --
826:    * the session may be in a state that is difficult to roll back without confusing the Gadget.
827:    * The Overseer will take care of the restart, possibly after rejecting other actions.
828:    */
829:   rejectAction(action: number): Promise<void | {restart?: boolean}>;
830: 
831:   /**
832:    * Attempts to revert an action that was already applied.
833:    *
834:    * Gatekeepers are not required to implement this. If unimplemented, the user will be instructed
835:    * that they need to perform the revert manually based on the action description. High-quality
836:    * gatekeepers should almost always implement this, though.
837:    *
838:    * If the returned `message` is non-null, it is Markdown to be displayed to the user. This may
839:    * be used, for example:
840:    * - To give the user additional instructions on how to complete the revert, if not all of it
841:    *   could be done automatically.
842:    * - To explain to the user why a revert is not possible, e.g. if other stacked modifications
843:    *   have been made on top which must be reverted first. (`canRetry` may be true in this case.)
844:    *
845:    * `canRetry` should be true if the revert failed (for a reason described in `message`), but
846:    * it could make sense to retry later. In this case the UI will continue to give the user the
847:    * option to revert.
848:    *
849:    * `restart` has the same meaning as for `rejectAction()`.
850:    */
851:   revertAction(action: number):
852:       Promise<void | {message?: string, canRetry?: boolean, restart?: boolean}>;
853: }
854: 
855: export interface ObservationAuthorizer extends RpcTarget {
856:   /**
857:    * Check whether the gadget should be permitted to make an observation (that is, to read some
858:    * data from an external service). The gatekeeper calls this on every read operation, and must
859:    * wait for the response before returning anything to the gadget. The method will return normally
860:    * if the operation is permitted, or throw an exception if not; the exception should propagate
861:    * through to the gadget.
862:    *
863:    * In many cases, the gatekeeper should actually call this *after* fetching the data from the
864:    * remote service, so that the description can include details about the actual data. As long
865:    * as the operation is strictly read-only, and the call is made before actually returning any
866:    * data to the gadget, this is OK.
867:    */
868:   authorizeObservation(description: ObservationDescription): Promise<void>;
869: }

871: /**
872:  * Macro expansion produced by a slash command. An absent message suppresses the generated
873:  * agent-visible message and agent turn; the visible command event remains in chat history.
874:  */
875: export type SlashCommandResult = {
876:   /** Optional skill name for the display badge. Commands that do not represent skills omit it. */
877:   skillName?: string;
878: 
879:   /**
880:    * Final text to insert into chat as if the user had sent it. The provider owns all formatting and
881:    * argument handling; Workshop stores this as an ordinary generated user message.
882:    */
883:   message?: string;
884: };
885: 
886: /** One slash command offered by a Gatekeeper. This is picker metadata only. */
887: export type SlashCommandDescriptor = {
888:   /** Opaque ID local to this provider. Passed back to invoke(). */
889:   id: string;
890: 
891:   /** Name shown after `/` in the picker. */
892:   name: string;
893: 
894:   /** Short description shown in the picker. */
895:   description: string;
896: 
897:   /** Optional label for the underlying resource (e.g. a collection path), used when names collide. */
898:   resourceLabel?: string;
899: };
900: 
901: /**
902:  * Optional API for a Gatekeeper that offers slash commands.
903:  *
904:  * list() returns non-sensitive picker metadata. Before invoke() returns expansion text derived from
905:  * protected data, it must use `authorizer` to authorize and audit the read. The provider cannot
906:  * submit actions or bind hooks.
907:  */
908: export interface SlashCommandProvider extends RpcTarget {
909:   /**
910:    * Complete catalog of commands offered by this provider. Providers should keep this reasonably
911:    * small.
912:    */
913:   list(): Promise<SlashCommandDescriptor[]>;
914: 
915:   /**
916:    * Runs the command identified by `id`, which must be an ID previously returned by list().
917:    * `args` is the unparsed natural-language text following the command. The provider owns all
918:    * expansion semantics and may return final text to insert as an ordinary user message.
919:    * `authorizer` remains authorization and audit only. The provider must reject unknown IDs.
920:    */
921:   invoke(
922:     id: string,
923:     args: string,
924:     authorizer: RpcStub<ObservationAuthorizer>,
925:   ): Promise<SlashCommandResult>;
926: }
927: 
928: /**
929:  * Used by a gatekeeper to request an action that has side effects (is not read-only). Any such
930:  * action may be subject to human-in-the-loop approval and audit logging. Whether or not review is
931:  * actually required, the gatekeeper must still submit all actions and wait for apply() to be
932:  * called before applying them.
933:  */
934: export interface ApprovalQueue extends ObservationAuthorizer {
935:   // TODO: Method to indicate that the gadget tried to perform an action that the gatekeeper itself
936:   //   hasn't been authorized to do (e.g. the user hasn't authorized the right OAuth scopes). The
937:   //   system should direct the user to the right UI to authorize the action.
938: 
939:   /**
940:    * Submit an action for approval.
941:    *
942:    * Unlike `authorizeObservation()`, `submitAction()` is fully asynchronous. It returns
943:    * immediately (that is, the returned Promise resolves quickly), but the action may not actually
944:    * be carried out until much later. It's intended that the user might not approve actions until
945:    * hours or days later, but this shouldn't cause any problems.
946:    *
947:    * `action` is a sequential integer action ID assigned by the gatekeeper. It will be passed back
948:    * to the Gatekeeper's applyAction() or rejectAction() when the action is later approved or
949:    * rejected.
950:    *
951:    * `description` describes the action in a way that can direct UI representation and policy
952:    * enforcement details.
953:    *
954:    * TODO: It would be nice if we can link this with the output gate so that if the submission
955:    *   does not complete, any SQL writes performed just before submit() are rolled back...
956:    */
957:   submitAction(action: number, description: ActionDescription): Promise<void>;
958: 
959:   /**
960:    * Notifies the overseer that the gadget (or an agent) has requested to register a persistent
961:    * callback hook.
962:    *
963:    * `callback` is the stub received from the Gadget, which is intended to be called whenever some
964:    * event occurs. Although `callback` is always a persistent stub (see below), the gatekeeper
965:    * should NOT try to store it on its own; it should always pass it to `bindHook` for the overseer
966:    * to store. Why? Because the callback needs to be bound to a particular gatekeeper *session*.
967:    * At the time you are calling `bindHook()`, the callback is tied to the session that is tied
968:    * to the `ApprovalQueue`. But that session will end at some point, after which the callback stub
969:    * you received is revoked. When you call HookInitiator.startHook() later on, that actually
970:    * initiates a *new* session (returning a new `ApprovalQueue`), and the callback returned then
971:    * is tied to that session instead.
972:    *
973:    * `controller` is an object implemented by the gatekeeper which allows the overseer to enable
974:    * or disable the hook.
975:    *
976:    * The hook is not immediately enabled, as the user may need to approve it first. If and when
977:    * the user has approved, the overseer will call controller.enable() to request that the the
978:    * gatekeeper begin delivering hook events. If the user never approves, no call will ever be
979:    * made. Therefore, the gatekeeper should avoid storing any state until the hook is enabled.
980:    * Typically, the `HookController` implementation should capture all information it needs to
981:    * register the hook into `props` so that it doesn't need to store anything elsewhere.
982:    *
983:    * In a typical implementation, the gatekeeper may expose an API to the gadget like:
984:    *
985:    *     onSomeEvent(callback: RpcStub<SomeInterface>)
986:    *
987:    * Where `SomeInterface` can be either an RpcTarget-derived interface, or a function type, but
988:    * either way the stub must be a persistent stub (see below). The gadget could call `onSomeEvent`
989:    * directly, but more commonly an agent will call it in a one-off `executeCode` tool call, since
990:    * this is usually one-time setup, not something that happens programmatically. The
991:    * implementation of `onSomeEvent` constructs a `HookController` implementation whose `props`
992:    * specify the details of the event to be hooked, then calls `bindHook()` to register the hook.
993:    * When the user approves, the overseer calls `controller.enable()`, which takes the provided
994:    * `HookInitiator` object and stores it somewhere where it can be invoked whenever "SomeEvent"
995:    * occurs. When the event occurs, first the gatekeeper calls `hookInitiator.startHook()` to
996:    * notify the overseer that a hook is incoming. The overseer returns back the original `callback`
997:    * stub along with an `ApprovalQueue`. Next the gatekeeper calls `authorizeObservation()` on the
998:    * `ApprovalQueue` -- since a hook invocation is almost always an observation of some sort.
999:    * Finally, it invokes the `callback` object to deliver the event to the gadget.
1000:    *
1001:    * Persistent stubs are (as of this writing) a relatively new feature of the Workers Runtime.
1002:    * A worker can construct an `RpcStub` that is "persistent", meaning it can be stored into
1003:    * Durable Object storage, as well as be used as part of the `props` for a WorkerEntrypoint. To
1004:    * create such a stub, the worker:
1005:    * 1. Implements a `[restore](params)` method, then
1006:    * 2. Calls `ctx.restore(params)` to invoke that method.
1007:    *
1008:    *     import {restore, RpcTarget, DurableObject} from "cloudflare:workers";
1009:    *
1010:    *     class Gadget extends DurableObject {
1011:    *       [restore]({type: string, greeting: string}) {
1012:    *         switch (type) {
1013:    *           case "greeter":
1014:    *             return new Greeter(greeting);
1015:    *           default:
1016:    *             throw new Error("unknown restore params");
1017:    *         }
1018:    *       }
1019:    *
1020:    *       async registerSomeHook() {
1021:    *         // Create a persistent stub.
1022:    *         let callback = await this.ctx.restore({type: "greeter", greeting: "Hello"});
1023:    *
1024:    *         // Register it against a hook offered by some gatekeeper API.
1025:    *         await this.env.SOME_GATEKEEPER.onSomeEventHook(callback);
1026:    *       }
1027:    *     }
1028:    *
1029:    *     // Some sort of RpcTarget implementation (just an example).
1030:    *     class Greeter extends RpcTarget {
1031:    *       constructor(greeting) {
1032:    *         super();
1033:    *         this.greeting = greeting;
1034:    *       }
1035:    *       greet(name) {
1036:    *         return `${this.greeting}, ${name}!`;
1037:    *       }
1038:    *     }
1039:    *
1040:    * The idea here is that `ctx.restore(params)` creates a *persistent* stub which can be
1041:    * re-created any time it is needed by calling the `[restore]()` method with the same params
